skill.name: benchmark-kernel
skill.description: Benchmark FlashInfer attention, GEMM, and MoE kernels with reproducible parameters, correctness checks, CUPTI timing, CUDA event fallback, and CSV output.
skill.summary: Run reproducible FlashInfer kernel benchmarks with accurate GPU timing and backend comparisons.
skill.author: flashinfer-ai

security_audit.summary: Eighty-four Ruby or shell backtick findings and the network-reconnaissance finding are false positives caused by Markdown formatting and benchmark arguments. The sudo nvidia-smi example is a real privileged system change that can alter GPU clocks for all workloads, although it contains no injection path. No malicious intent, prompt injection, or data exfiltration was found.

remediation.suggestion: Remove sudo from the default workflow. Document operator approval, shared-system impact, required permissions, and a clock-reset procedure for advanced users.

content.value_statement: GPU kernel comparisons are unreliable when timing methods and parameters vary. This skill guides reproducible FlashInfer benchmarks using CUPTI or CUDA events.
actual_capabilities: Guides single and batch benchmarks through flashinfer_benchmark.py.
Configures attention, FP8 GEMM, and MoE routines across supported backends.
Explains CUPTI timing and automatic CUDA event fallback.
Applies reference checks, warmups, measurement iterations, and reproducer generation.
Shows custom Python timing with bench_gpu_time.
Interprets median latency, variation, throughput, bandwidth, and CSV results.
limitations: Examples require a FlashInfer source checkout, a supported NVIDIA GPU, and a working CUDA environment.
The preferred CUPTI path requires CUDA 13 or later and a compatible cupti-python package.
Hardware and backend compatibility must be checked against the current FlashInfer support matrix.
The skill provides instructions only; it does not execute benchmarks or validate measured results.

use_cases.title: Compare Kernel Backends
use_cases.description: Measure identical attention or GEMM shapes across supported backends with correctness checks and consistent timing.

use_cases.title: Build Repeatable Benchmark Suites
use_cases.description: Run parameterized test lists, preserve reproducer details, and save metrics for later analysis.

use_cases.title: Design Custom Timing Studies
use_cases.description: Use bench_gpu_time for controlled experiments with warmups, iteration counts, cache behavior, and timing selection.

prompt_templates.title: Start a FlashInfer Benchmark
prompt_templates.prompt: Prepare a minimal FlashInfer decode-attention benchmark for my [GPU] using [backends]. Include prerequisites, reference checking, timing behavior, and result interpretation.
prompt_templates.scenario: Run a first benchmark with clear defaults.

prompt_templates.title: Compare Kernel Backends
prompt_templates.prompt: Build a fair comparison for [routine] across [backends] using [shape and data types]. Keep inputs, warmups, iterations, and validation identical.
prompt_templates.scenario: Evaluate backend performance for one workload.

prompt_templates.title: Plan a Batch Benchmark
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a batch benchmark plan covering [workloads]. Define the test matrix, CSV fields, correctness checks, reproducer details, and comparison criteria.

prompt_templates.title: Design a Custom Timing Study
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a bench_gpu_time experiment for [kernel]. Address CUPTI fallback, cache state, statistical stability, operation counts, throughput calculations, and likely measurement bias.

output_examples.input: Compare FA2 and cuDNN for one decode-attention shape on an H100.
output: Benchmark plan: compare both backends on identical shapes with five warmups and thirty measured iterations.
Validation: enable reference checking and record median latency, variation, throughput, and reproducer details.

output_examples.input: My kernel latency changes significantly between runs.
output: Diagnosis: review warmup count, GPU load, clock behavior, cache state, and timing method.
Next steps: increase warmups and iterations, isolate competing workloads, then compare median latency and variation.

output_examples.input: I need a custom timing study for a new FlashInfer kernel.
output: Design: wrap the kernel with stable inputs and measure it through bench_gpu_time.
Report: include timing mode, cache policy, iteration counts, latency statistics, operation count, and calculated throughput.

best_practices: Enable reference checking before trusting performance comparisons.
Record GPU model, software versions, parameters, warmups, and measurement iterations.
Use identical inputs and timing methods when comparing backends.
anti_patterns: Do not compare results collected with different shapes, data types, or timing methods.
Do not treat one iteration as representative performance.
Do not use output mismatches as valid performance evidence.

faq.question: Does this skill run benchmarks automatically?
faq.answer: No. It provides commands, parameter guidance, and interpretation steps for a FlashInfer checkout with compatible CUDA hardware.

faq.question: Is CUPTI required?
faq.answer: No. FlashInfer can fall back to CUDA events, but CUPTI provides more direct GPU kernel timing.

faq.question: Which kernel families are covered?
faq.answer: The guide covers attention, FP8 and FP4 GEMM, and mixture-of-experts routines listed by FlashInfer.

faq.question: Can the skill compare multiple backends?
faq.answer: Yes. It shows how to hold workload parameters constant while comparing supported FlashAttention, cuDNN, CUTLASS, cuBLAS, and TensorRT-LLM backends.

faq.question: Which results can I collect?
faq.answer: Typical results include median latency, standard deviation, effective throughput, memory bandwidth, CSV records, and reproducer details.

faq.question: How can I improve reproducibility?
faq.answer: Record hardware and software versions, use fixed parameters, include warmups, run multiple iterations, enable validation, and preserve reproducer details.
